claims.text: Minimal atomic size mismatch produces low intrinsic lattice strain in multimetallic nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with minimal atomic size mismatch will remain stable, single-phase solid solutions from 473 K to 1923 K.
High configurational entropy dominates the stability of low-strain, multimetallic solid solutions over the stated temperature range.
Larger atomic size mismatch causes strain-induced phase segregation or chemical ordering at high temperature.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous solid solutions containing five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
Changing nanoparticle composition can systematically tune atomic size mismatch while retaining the same number of metallic elements.
Atomic size mismatch governs the extent of lattice strain.
At low lattice strain, configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid solution at high temperature.
High lattice strain promotes differential atomic mobilities.
Strain relaxation at high lattice strain leads to phase segregation or chemically ordered structures as the system lowers its free energy.
Low-mismatch nanoparticles will retain consistent lattice parameters and uniform elemental distributions throughout 473–1923 K.
High-mismatch nanoparticles will exhibit detectable phase separation or chemical ordering near 1923 K.
The prediction applies only when synthesis and initial thermal treatment are held constant and extrinsic chemical interactions do not dominate.
Surface-energy effects and kinetic barriers may influence structural and chemical stability.
Failure of high-mismatch nanoparticles to show segregation or ordering near 1923 K relative to low-mismatch controls would falsify the proposed strain-governed stability mechanism.
